docs.title: Developer docs
docs.text: A provider can live in the server repository, where it ships with every Music Assistant server, or in a repository of your own, from which servers install it through the community catalog. Building a provider tells what each place asks and how to build a provider in your own repository. This page sets up the server repository and describes building a provider inside it.

docs.title: 📝 Prerequisites
docs.text:
• ffmpeg (minimum version 8.0), must be available in the path so install at OS level
  • Python 3.14 is minimal required (the exact pinned runtime is in .python-version in the server repository)
  • Python venv

We recommend developing on a (recent) macOS or Linux machine. It is recommended to use Visual Studio Code as your IDE, since launch files to start Music Assistant are provided as part of the repository. Furthermore, the current code base is not verified to work on a native Windows machine. If you would like to develop on a Windows machine, install WSL2 to increase your swag-level 🤘.

docs.title: Python venv (recommended)
docs.text:
With this repository cloned locally, execute the following commands in a terminal from the root of your repository:

  • Run our development setup script to setup the development environment:
  • scripts/setup.sh (creates a new separate virtual environment to nicely separate the project dependencies)
  • The setup script will create a separate virtual environment (if needed), install all the project/test dependencies and configure pre-commit for linting and testing.
  • Make sure, that the python interpreter in VS Code is set to the newly generated venv.
  • Debug: Hit (Fn +) F5 to start Music Assistant locally
  • The pre-compiled UI of Music Assistant will be available at localhost:8095 🎉

NOTE: Always re-run the setup script after you fetch the latest code because requirements could have changed.

docs.title: Using Devcontainer/Codespace
docs.text: We removed support for devcontainers because we do not have anyone willing to maintain it. It also is not very convenient due to all the port requirements, binaries etc. If somebody is willing to create and maintain a devcontainer with host networking and based on our base alpine image, we will add the support back. Until then: Develop with Python venv on a Linux or macOS machine (see above).

docs.title: Developing on the Music Assistant Server Models
docs.text:
If you're working on core Music Assistant features, you may need to modify the shared data models. The Python models which are shared between client and server are located in the music-assistant/models repository, while the corresponding client-side TypeScript interfaces are in interfaces.ts in the Frontend repository.

In most cases, you won't need to modify the models. However, if you do need to make changes, here's how to set up your development environment to use a local models repository instead of the one installed via pip:

  • First, clone the models repository to your local machine.

  • Then, install your local models clone in "editable" mode. This allows your changes to be reflected immediately without a reinstall. Run the following command from the server repository's root:

    uv pip install -e /path/to/your/cloned/models/repo --config-settings editable_mode=strict

Note

You must rerun this command whenever you add or remove files from the models repository to ensure the changes are picked up.

docs.title: Note on async Python
docs.text: The Music Assistant server is fully built in Python. The Python language has no real supported for multi-threading. This is why Music Assistant heavily relies on asyncio to handle blocking IO. It is important to get a good understanding of asynchronous programming before building your first provider. This video is an excellent first step in the world of asyncio.

docs.title: Building a new Music Provider
docs.text:
A Music Provider is the provider type that adds support for a 'source of music' to Music Assistant. Spotify and Youtube Music are examples of a Music Provider, but also Filesystem and SMB can be put in the Music Provider category. All Providers (of all types) can be found in the music_assistant/providers folder.

TIP: We have created a template/stub "Demo Music Provider" implementation in music_assistant/providers/_demo_music_provider to help you get started faster with building your new Music Provider for Music Assistant server!

Adding the necessary files for a new Music Provider

Add a new folder to the providers folder with the name of provider. Add two files inside:

  1. __init__.py. This file contains the Python code of your provider.
  2. manifest.json. This file contains metadata and configuration for your provider.

Configuring the manifest.json file

The easiest way to get start is to copy the contents of the manifest of an existing Music Provider, e.g. Spotify or Youtube Music. See the manifest section for all available properties.

Creating the provider

Create a file called __init__.py inside the folder of your provider. This file will contain the logic for the provider. All Music Providers must inherit from the MusicProvider base class and override the necessary functions where applicable. A few things to note:

  • The setup() function is called by Music Assistant upon initialization of the provider. It gives you the opportunity the prepare the provider for usage.
  • Anything interactive (credentials, OAuth logins, pairing) belongs in a setup flow; runtime options are declared by overriding get_config_entries() on the provider.
  • A provider should let Music Assistant know which ProviderFeature it supports by implementing the property supported_features, which returns a list of ProviderFeature.
  • List the media types the provider offers whatever its config or account in the provides of its manifest, such as radio for a radio directory. It is for discovery only: what the provider does always comes from its code.
  • The actual playback of audio in Music Assistant happens in two phases:
    1. get_stream_details() is called to obtain information about the audio, like the quality, format, # of channels etc.
    2. get_audio_stream() is called to stream raw bytes of audio to the player. There are a few helpers to help you with this. Note that this function is not applicable to direct url streams.
  • Examples:
    1. Streaming raw bytes using an external executable (librespot) to get audio, see the Spotify provider as an example
    2. Streaming a direct URL, see the Youtube Music provider as an example
    3. Streaming an https stream that uses an expiring URL, see the Qobuz provider as an example

docs.title: ▶️ Building your own Player Provider
docs.text:
A Player Provider is the provider type that adds support for a 'target of playback' to Music Assistant. Sonos, Chromecast and AirPlay are examples of a Player Provider. All Providers (of all types) can be found in the music_assistant/providers folder.

TIP: We have created a template/stub "Demo Player Provider" implementation in music_assistant/providers/_demo_player_provider to help get you started faster with building your own Player Provider for Music Assistant server!

docs.title: 💽 Building your own Metadata Provider
docs.text:
A Metadata Provider is the provider type that provides additional metadata which is missing from the preliminary items obtained from the music provider sources. They supplement metadata in the Music Assistant server database by importing information or album artwork from other online sources that are then added to the library. For example, the metadata providers for MusicBrainz, fanart.tv, and Cover Art Archive. Note that metadata providers do NOT change anything (e.g. ID3 tags) obtained from the original item.

More information and template/stub demo metadata provider to follow.

docs.title: 🔌 Building your own Plugin Provider
docs.text:
A Plugin Provider is the provider type that provides additional functionality to Music Assistant and most often it will interact with the existing core controllers and event logic. For example a music scrobbling plugin such as the LastFM Scrobbler Plugin (that lets you scrobble songs and albums you listen to LastFM and LibreFM), or the AirPlay Receiver Plugin (that enable you to add AirPlay Receiver audio support to any MA player), or the Home Assistant Plugin Provider (that provides a connection from the Music Assistant integration running in Home Assistant to Music Assistant server that allow exposing HA players so that they become visible in MA).

TIP: We have created a template/stub "Demo Plugin Provider" implementation in music_assistant/providers/_demo_plugin_provider to help get you started faster with building your own Plugin Provider for Music Assistant server!

docs.title: ⚙️ Manifest file
docs.text:
The manifest file contains metadata and configuration about a provider. The supported properties are:

Name Description Type type music, player, metadata, plugin or audio_analysis string domain The internal unique id of the provider, e.g. spotify or ytmusic string name The full name of the provider, e.g. Spotify or Youtube Music string description The full description of the provider string codeowners List of Github names of the codeowners of the provider array[string] requirements Python packages the provider needs, in standard pip / PEP 508 requirement syntax, e.g. package==version, a version range, an extras marker, or a git+https://… direct reference array[string] documentation URL to the provider's documentation page. string multi_instance Whether multiple instances of the provider are supported, e.g. multiple user accounts for Spotify boolean provides Optional, for discovery only, such as the filters of the Marketplace: what the provider offers whatever its config. A music provider lists media types: artist, album, track, playlist, radio, podcast, audiobook or sound_effect. A plugin lists its main features: audio_source (plays audio into Music Assistant), ai (provides AI engines), tts (provides speech engines), scrobble, assistant (lets an AI or voice assistant control Music Assistant), visualizer, recommendations or fun; one that lists none is a generic plugin. A player provider can list audio_source. What a provider does at runtime always comes from its code. array[string]

This table lists the main properties; the developer guide of the server has the full, current table.

Provider configuration is not declared in the manifest: interactive setup (credentials, OAuth, pairing) is authored as a setup flow, and runtime options are declared in code by overriding get_config_entries() — see Provider setup flows.

docs.title: Building a provider
docs.text: A provider adds something to Music Assistant: a music source, support for a kind of player, a metadata source or a plugin. A provider can live in two places, and what each asks of you differs.

docs.title: In the server repository: a built-in provider
docs.text:
A built-in provider ships with every Music Assistant server, and the team keeps it working through every change to the server. Because the project supports it for years, a new built-in provider asks for:

  • demand you can show: users who want it, beyond yourself;
  • a pull request on the user documentation that describes it;
  • code that follows the code standards of the server and the usage policy, with tests;
  • a named maintainer (you) who follows up on issues and on changes to the service, the device or the server.

You work in a fork of the server, and a maintainer reviews the new provider against the usage policy. After that, you merge most changes to your own provider yourself through the review bot. A built-in provider whose maintainer no longer follows up may be moved to the community catalog; that is announced first, so someone can take it over. The contributing guide and the developer guide of the server have the details, and the front page of this site sets up a development environment for the server.

docs.title: In your own repository: a community provider
docs.text:
A community provider lives in your own repository, with your own documentation, support and releases. Servers install it from the community catalog, a list the project keeps in the registry. Only an administrator sees the community catalog, in the Marketplace, after enabling it and accepting that everything in it is installed at their own risk; other users only see what was installed from it.

The community catalog asks less than the server repository, and the project supports nothing in it:

  • a public repository with an open source licence;
  • releases that pass the automated checks;
  • a domain of its own (the unique id of the provider in its manifest.json, such as sample_music, not a domain name): not one the server uses or reserves, and not one another community provider has;
  • a provider that crosses none of the red lines below.

A person decides once, at admission, about what the provider does. The code is not reviewed, and later releases reach users without anyone looking at them.

docs.title: The red lines
docs.text:
The community catalog declines a provider at admission, and blocks it when it is found later, when it crosses one of the red lines in the community catalog rules, which also say what is allowed at the user's own risk.

A server stops loading a blocked provider once its next daily check of the community catalog fetches the block; its users keep their settings and library. A blocked version is skipped the same way.

docs.title: The template
docs.text:
The community provider template is where a community provider starts. It holds one small music source, a test that runs it in a real server, a development container and CI. Its README takes you from Use this template to a provider running in a server in a few minutes, with Docker and VS Code with the Dev Containers extension as the only requirements, on Windows, macOS or Linux.

The template pins the server version you develop against, at a release tag or a commit, and installs it from its source, which gives you type checking, completion in your editor and the test fixture.

What a release has to look like:

  • the provider is in a folder named after its domain, provider, or providers/<domain> in a repository with several providers;
  • the release is a GitHub release, not a pre-release, whose tag is the version with or without v, such as v1.2.0;
  • the requirements are package names with version specifiers, without URLs, markers or options, and come as wheels for the Python version and platform of the server: a package that only comes as source cannot be installed;
  • the manifest is plain JSON;
  • the icon is optional: an SVG of at most 5 KB that only draws; an icon that does not pass is left out.

The registry lists the exact limits in What a provider needs.

Once installed, a provider runs inside the user's server. It never writes into its own folder: the server checks that folder against the release and replaces it when it differs. Options are config entries (get_config_entries), values that repeat go in the server's cache (@use_cache, self.mass.cache), and files go in a folder of its own under self.mass.storage_path or self.mass.cache_path. Its requirements are installed next to the server's own packages and never replace one; a provider whose requirements clash is not loaded.

docs.title: Where users get help
docs.text: The support_url in the manifest is where you take questions and bug reports, such as the issues of your repository. The Get help button of the app, on the settings page of the provider and in its details in the Marketplace, opens it, and so does the link to its maintainers in the note the app shows before it installs a provider from the community catalog. Without a support_url, the server gives an installed community provider its repository as one, so questions reach you and not the support repository of Music Assistant. The app only follows a link that starts with https://.

docs.title: In your repository
docs.text:
uv run pytest runs the tests of the template: quick checks of the manifest, the texts, the requirements and the icon, and a test that boots a real server with your repository as its local provider folder. The fixture comes with the server: pytest_plugins = ["music_assistant.testing"] in tests/conftest.py gives a fixture mass, a started server in dev mode with your repository as its local provider folder. That server announces nothing on the network and listens only on the local machine; what your provider asks of its service still goes out, so replace that in a test where you need to. The fixture needs pytest-asyncio with asyncio_mode = "auto", and next to the server the requirements of its Sendspin provider (aiosendspin[server] and av, at the versions in the server's music_assistant/providers/sendspin/manifest.json), which the server starts at every boot. The template has all of this in place.

scripts/run.sh, or the Run Music Assistant task in VS Code, starts a server in dev mode that loads your provider, so you can try it in the app. Outside the container, on macOS or Linux with uv and ffmpeg 8 or newer, this is:

uv sync
scripts/run.sh

Only a server in dev mode loads providers from a local folder.

docs.title: On your pull requests
docs.text: CI runs the lint, the type check, the spelling check and your tests, and calls the registry's reusable workflow check-provider.yml, which runs the same checks the community catalog runs on a release: the manifest, the requirements against a channel, and loading the provider in the server image of that channel. Loading installs the requirements and imports the module of the provider; it does not set the provider up and does not run your tests.

docs.title: On a Music Assistant server
docs.text:
Before you release, you can try your provider on a real Music Assistant server that fetches it from GitHub. This server runs the nightly build of Music Assistant, and the community catalog does not have to be enabled on it. Your repository must be public, with the provider in a folder named after its domain, provider, or providers/<domain> in a repository with several providers. You name it in one of these forms:

  • owner/repo: its default branch;
  • owner/repo@ref: a branch, a tag or a commit;
  • owner/repo@pr-12: pull request 12 of that repository.

The server fetches your repository again at every start, so a restart picks up new commits. Your provider then appears among the providers you can add, with the badge Community. When it does not, the log of the server tells why.

Use a test server with data of its own, never the data of the server you use every day.

docs.title: On Home Assistant
docs.text:
1. In the App store of Home Assistant, add the repository https://github.com/music-assistant/home-assistant-addon when it is not there yet, and install the Music Assistant DEV SERVER app.
  2. Stop the Music Assistant app if it runs: the two apps use the same network ports.
  3. In the Configuration tab of the DEV SERVER app, set Provider repository to your repository, such as your-github-handle/your-repository@my-branch, and start the app.
  4. Select Open Web UI and add your provider.

The DEV SERVER app keeps data of its own, apart from the Music Assistant app. Its Log tab shows the log of the server; set Log Level to debug for more detail. To go back, stop the DEV SERVER app and start the Music Assistant app again.

docs.title: On Docker
docs.text:
Stop any other Music Assistant server on the machine first: both would use the same network ports. Then start the development image with your repository and a volume of its own:

docker run --rm --network host -v ma-dev-data:/data \
  -e PROVIDER_REPO=your-github-handle/your-repository@my-branch \
  ghcr.io/music-assistant/server:dev
  • Open port 8095 of the machine in a browser and add your provider.
  • The container prints the log of the server; add --log-level debug after the image name for more detail.
  • To restart, stop the container with Ctrl+C and run the command again.
  • To go back, stop the container and start your own server again.
  • docker volume rm ma-dev-data removes the data of the test server.

docs.title: Joining the community catalog
docs.text:
You submit your provider with the form Submit a provider: its repository, and only when needed the folder and the tag prefix. The person who submits it must own the repository or be a code owner in the manifest of its latest release, and that release must pass the checks on at least one channel. The result of the checks appears as a comment on the issue. When every check passes, a registry maintainer reviews the provider against the rules and decides. The owner of the repository and the code owners in the manifest are the maintainers of the provider. The registry's README tells the rest.

Moving a provider from the server. A code owner of a provider that ships with the server can move it to their own repository under the same domain: submit it with the box Moving from the server ticked. Once it is admitted, the team removes it from the server in the release whose community catalog offers it, and servers that use it then install your version and keep their settings. While the server still ships the domain, the test fixture and a server in dev mode do not load your copy: the server already has a provider by that name.

Providers without a maintainer. A built-in provider whose maintainer no longer follows up is parked in a repository of the Music Assistant organisation and keeps being released through the community catalog. To take it over, say so on its issue "looking for a maintainer"; you then release it from your own repository under the same domain.

docs.title: What the nightly test reports
docs.text:
You release whenever you want: publish a GitHub release, and nothing else is needed. The registry looks for new releases once a night: it takes the most recently published release of each listed provider, when it has not seen it before, and checks it. It also tests the newest versions of each provider again against the current server of every channel it tests: the nightly, the beta and the newest stable channel.

  • A version that passes on a channel is offered to the servers on that channel.
  • A version that fails, or that stops loading on a channel, is not offered there. Servers on that channel that run it switch to the newest version that still passes there; when none does, the provider stops loading there.
  • A release that is refused or fails, and a version that stops loading on a channel, are reported in one issue per provider on the registry, with the label release-check, the reason and the output of the failing check. The issue mentions the maintainers of the provider once, a later failure is added to it as a comment, and it closes by itself when a later release passes.

With a beta that runs for several weeks, you usually know about a problem well before a stable release reaches your users. To support the stable release and follow the nightly at the same time, publish one version, wait until the registry has picked it up (it appears under providers/<domain>/ in the registry), and then publish the other. Each version is then offered where it passes.

docs.title: Listing contract
docs.text:
Music Assistant listing commands share a contract for sorting, filtering and paging. The server is authoritative for which sort fields each listing supports; clients should discover those options instead of assuming that every listing offers the same fields.

The contract ships with server 2.11. Older servers do not have music/sort_options or the typed sort arguments. The Python client checks the minimum API schema for each argument and raises InvalidServerVersion when the server is too old.

docs.title: Discover sort options
docs.text:
Call music/sort_options with a ListingType. The response is a list of SortOptionInfo values; the default option is first. Each option identifies its SortField, whether direction is supported, and its default direction when applicable.

from music_assistant_models.enums import ListingType, SortDirection, SortField

options = await client.music.get_sort_options(ListingType.LIBRARY_TRACKS)
by_name = next((o for o in options if o.field == SortField.NAME), options[0])
tracks = await client.music.get_library_tracks(
    limit=100,
    offset=0,
    sort_field=by_name.field,
    sort_direction=SortDirection.ASC if by_name.supports_direction else None,
)

Typed sorting is available on library listings and supported detail listings, including album, artist, genre, playlist and podcast contents, browse results, similar tracks and media versions. Pass sort_direction only when the selected option supports it; the server ignores it otherwise. Omit either sort argument to use the listing's default. A sort_field the listing does not offer fails with InvalidDataError.

docs.title: Pagination and filtering
docs.text:
Listing methods accept limit and offset where paging is supported. search and listing-specific filters can be combined with paging and sorting. In particular, music/playlists/playlist_tracks and music/podcasts/podcast_episodes return one page as a list, with a default limit of 500 and an offset of 0. Request subsequent pages by advancing offset; these commands no longer produce chunked results.

The Python client exposes these as ordinary list-returning methods:

page_size = 100
offset = 0
while page := await client.music.get_podcast_episodes(
    podcast_id,
    provider,
    limit=page_size,
    offset=offset,
):
    process(page)
    offset += len(page)

docs.title: Random ordering
docs.text:
For listings that offer SortField.RANDOM, pass the same integer random_seed on every page in a single listing load. This keeps the order stable while paging. Use a new seed to request a new random order. A seed does not freeze the underlying data, and the server remains authoritative for whether a listing offers random sorting. random_seed requires API schema 98; the Python client checks this minimum when the argument is set.

seed = 4217
first_page = await client.music.get_library_tracks(
    limit=100,
    offset=0,
    sort_field=SortField.RANDOM,
    random_seed=seed,
)
second_page = await client.music.get_library_tracks(
    limit=100,
    offset=100,
    sort_field=SortField.RANDOM,
    random_seed=seed,
)

See the server's random listing notes for details.

docs.title: Playback sorting
docs.text: player_queues/play_media accepts sort_field and sort_direction to order album or playlist tracks before applying start_item. Use the same sort field offered by the corresponding listing; any other field fails with InvalidDataError. The deprecated sort_by string is retained for older clients only.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
• Replace order_by with sort_field and, where supported, sort_direction.
  • Replace playback sort_by with sort_field and sort_direction.
  • Replace chunked playlist-track and podcast-episode consumption with repeated paged calls using limit and offset; each response is a list containing at most one page.
  • Discover supported fields with music/sort_options instead of hard-coding a sort list.

docs.title: Provider setup flows
docs.text:
Music Assistant separates interactive setup from runtime options:

  • Setup flow — everything needed to get a provider or player working: credentials, OAuth logins, pairing PINs, discovery choices. Authored as a small coroutine in providers/<domain>/setup_flow.py, driven step-by-step by the server, rendered by the frontend in a dialog. The values a flow collects are stored as the target's setup_data: encrypted at rest and never serialized over the API.
  • Options — the runtime knobs (quality, behavior toggles, output settings). Declared by overriding get_config_entries() on the provider (or player) instance and stored as regular config values.

If your provider needs no interaction to set up (works out of the box, or only needs options), don't create a setup_flow.py — the add-provider UI then completes immediately. Providers that are auto-created by the server (builtin) must not have one.

docs.title: Quick start: a credential flow
docs.text:
# providers/myprovider/setup_flow.py
from music_assistant_models.config_entries import ConfigEntry
from music_assistant_models.enums import ConfigEntryType

from music_assistant.models.setup_flow import SetupSession

_ENTRIES = [
    ConfigEntry(key="username", type=ConfigEntryType.STRING, label="Username", required=True),
    ConfigEntry(key="password", type=ConfigEntryType.SECURE_STRING, label="Password", required=True),
]


async def run_setup(session: SetupSession) -> None:
    """Run the interactive setup for this provider."""
    errors: dict[str, str] | None = None
    while True:
        values = await session.form(_ENTRIES, step_id="user", errors=errors, last_step=True)
        try:
            await _validate_login(str(values["username"]), str(values["password"]))
        except LoginFailed as err:
            # re-show the form with an error; the user can correct and retry
            errors = {"base": err.translation_key or str(err)}
            continue
        await session.finish(values)
        return

The engine calls run_setup(session) when the user starts the flow. Each await session.form(...) suspends the coroutine until the user submits; session.finish(values) persists the values as setup_data and creates (or reloads) the target. If loading fails, finish raises SetupFlowError — catch it and loop back to a form instead of dead-ending.

docs.title: The SetupSession API
docs.text:
Call Purpose await session.form(entries, step_id="user", errors=None, last_step=None, expires_in=None) Show a form, return the submitted values. errors maps entry keys (or "base") to error slugs/text for a retry round. last_step controls the submit button label. await session.external(url, step_id="auth", expires_in=None) Send the user to an external URL (OAuth). Resumes when the flow's callback_url is hit; returns the merged GET/POST callback params. session.progress(step_id, text=None, pct=None, image=None) Fire-and-forget display-only progress step. Re-emit it to update text, percentage, or image in place. await session.progress_until(awaitable, step_id, text=None, image=None, expires_in=None) Show progress while awaiting something, with a single deadline that drives both the UI countdown and the enforcement. Raises StepExpiredError on the deadline. await session.finish(values) Persist values as the target's setup_data, create/reload the target, publish the FINISH step. Raises SetupFlowError when the target fails to load with these values. raise AbortFlow(reason) End the flow with a translated message (setup_flow.abort.<reason>). Use for unrecoverable situations.

Everything the user sees is translatable — see Translations.

docs.title: Flow context
docs.text:
session.context describes what is being (re)configured:

  • kind — "setup" (new) or "reconfigure" (existing target)
  • reason — "user", "auth" (re-auth needed) or "error" (target failed to load)
  • instance_id / player_id — the existing target, for reconfigure and player flows
  • setup_data — the decrypted values from a previous run, for prefill
  • values — the target's current options values

A reconfigure flow is the same coroutine: branch on session.context.kind to prefill entries (set each entry's default_value from context.setup_data) or to skip steps that are already satisfied.

docs.title: Multi-step flows
docs.text:
Just call session.form() (or any other step) more than once. Collect values across steps in a local dict and pass the merged result to finish:

async def run_setup(session: SetupSession) -> None:
    collected: dict[str, ConfigValueType] = {}
    collected.update(await session.form(_SERVER_ENTRIES, step_id="server"))
    if collected.get("use_auth"):
        collected.update(await session.form(_CRED_ENTRIES, step_id="credentials"))
    await session.finish(collected)

Steps can expire: pass expires_in=<seconds> and the frontend shows a countdown while the engine enforces the deadline (StepExpiredError — catch it to mint a fresh code and re-show the step, as pairing and device-code flows do).

docs.title: OAuth / external login
docs.text:
async def run_setup(session: SetupSession) -> None:
    auth_url = build_authorize_url(redirect_uri=session.callback_url)
    params = await session.external(auth_url, step_id="authenticate")
    if "code" not in params:
        raise AbortFlow("auth_failed")
    tokens = await exchange_code(str(params["code"]))
    await session.finish({"refresh_token": tokens.refresh_token})

The frontend renders an "Open" button (plus the destination host as a trust cue) and waits. The external party — or a small bounce page you host — must redirect/POST to session.callback_url (/setup_flow/callback/<flow_id>); query and body parameters are handed back to your coroutine.

docs.title: Progress and inline images
docs.text:
ConfigEntryType.IMAGE entries and the image= argument accept a data URI, which the dialog renders inline — used for QR logins and device codes:

creds = await session.progress_until(
    client.poll_until_confirmed(device),
    step_id="device_login",
    text="device_login",
    image=render_code_svg(device.user_code),   # data:image/svg+xml;... URI
    expires_in=float(device.expires_in),
)

docs.title: Player setup flows
docs.text:
Players use the same session API. A player that needs interaction (pairing PIN, password) overrides run_setup_flow on its Player class and sets needs_setup/setup_reason so the UI shows a Setup required chip:

class MyPlayer(Player):
    async def run_setup_flow(self, session: SetupSession) -> None:
        pin_entry = [ConfigEntry(key="pin", type=ConfigEntryType.STRING, label="PIN", required=True)]
        await self._start_pairing()
        values = await session.form(pin_entry, step_id="pair", expires_in=60)
        await self._finish_pairing(str(values["pin"]))
        await session.finish({"credentials": self._credentials})

Wrapper players (universal players, native players wrapping protocol children) need no code: the engine delegates to the child that needs setup, or shows a picker when several do. The collected values persist to the child's own config.

Set setup_reason to a short slug ("pairing_required", "password_required", "auth_expired") — it resolves against the provider's translations and is shown on the chip.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text:
All flow-facing text lives in the provider's strings.json:

{
  "setup_flow": {
    "user": { "title": "Connect your account", "description": "Enter your credentials." },
    "device_login": { "progress_text": "Enter the code on the device page" },
    "abort": { "auth_failed": "Authentication failed." }
  },
  "errors": {
    "invalid_credentials": "Invalid username or password."
  }
}
  • setup_flow.<step_id>.title / .description — form and external steps
  • setup_flow.<step_id>.progress_text — progress steps (the text= argument is the key)
  • setup_flow.abort.<reason> — AbortFlow reasons
  • errors.<slug> — error slugs passed via errors= (owner-first resolution: your provider's file wins, then common)

docs.title: Runtime options
docs.text:
Options are declared on the provider (or player) instance — the method takes no arguments and reads whatever it needs from self:

class MyProvider(MusicProvider):
    async def get_config_entries(self) -> tuple[ConfigEntry, ...]:
        """Return the runtime options for this provider instance."""
        return (
            ConfigEntry(key="quality", type=ConfigEntryType.STRING, label="Quality", options=...),
        )

    async def handle_config_action(self, action: str) -> tuple[ConfigEntry, ...]:
        """Handle a one-shot action button press and re-render the entries."""
        if action == "clear_cache":
            await self._clear_cache()
            return await self.get_config_entries()
        return await super().handle_config_action(action)

ConfigEntryType.ACTION entries render as buttons; a press arrives via config/providers/invoke_action → handle_config_action(action). Actions are one-shot side effects on saved state — anything that needs input or multiple steps belongs in the setup flow. An action that must open a browser page returns a ConfigEntryType.URL entry in its response; the frontend opens it once and drops it from the form.

docs.title: API commands
docs.text:
Command Purpose config/providers/setup {provider_domain} Start the setup flow for a new provider instance config/providers/reconfigure {instance_id} Re-run the flow for an existing instance (also used for re-auth) config/players/setup {player_id} Start (or re-run) a player's setup flow config/flows/submit {flow_id, values} Submit the active step's values config/flows/get {flow_id} Re-fetch the current step (reconnects) config/flows/abort {flow_id} Abort a running flow config/providers/get_entries {instance_id} Options entries for an existing instance config/players/get_entries {player_id} Options entries for a player config/providers/invoke_action {instance_id, action} Run an options action button config/players/invoke_action {player_id, action} Run a player options action button

Flow steps are pushed as SETUP_FLOW_UPDATED events (translated per connection); sessions expire after 15 minutes of inactivity.

docs.title: Migrating older providers
docs.text:
If you maintain an out-of-tree provider, note what the setup-flows redesign removed:

  • AuthenticationHelper and the AUTH_SESSION event are gone. Use session.external() — it provides the callback route and the browser-open UX.
  • Actions can no longer tunnel through get_entries. get_config_entries takes no arguments; button presses arrive via handle_config_action. Multi-step "action flows" (intermediate values, session_id plumbing) are setup flows now.
  • Setup values moved out of the options namespace. Credentials collected by a flow live in setup_data (read via self.get_setup_value(key)), not in config values.
